name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,681

clue.text: Some might say Hoskins is immortal on drugs

indicators.note: letters that are on drugs are out of their heads, so the words 'is immortal' come out jumbled

blocks.note: the fodder: ten letters, all used

explanation.surface: A boast from the setter that he will live forever, as long as the pills keep coming.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is the setter, poking fun at himself: the surface brag about living forever hides the jibe that some think him an IMMORALIST, fitting for a puzzle full of sex and drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter imagines critics labelling him a person without morals, so the jibe they would aim at him is the definition.

clue.text: U2 member hugs old boy and promiscuous primate!

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap your arms round, so the band member wraps round 'old boy'

blocks.note: the lead singer of the Irish band U2
standard abbreviation for a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: A rock star embracing a former schoolmate, and then, absurdly, an ape of loose morals.
explanation.walkthrough: BONO splits after BON to take OB inside. 'Old boy' reads as a person in the surface but is the abbreviation OB.
explanation.definitionFit: This African ape, a close relative of the chimpanzee, is famous for using frequent sexual contact to settle social tension.

clue.text: Teen messing with gaol gets stretch

indicators.note: messing with something throws it into disorder, so 'teen' and 'gaol' get their letters jumbled

blocks.note: first half of the fodder
second half of the fodder; gaol is the British spelling of jail

explanation.surface: A delinquent youth who causes trouble in prison is rewarded with a longer sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' looks like prison slang for a sentence, which suits the gaol surface, but here it is the plain verb meaning to lengthen.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to make something longer by pulling or extending it, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: Books one brought to southern soul singer?

indicators.note: one thing brought to another is set beside it, so the pieces join end to end

blocks.note: the Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible
Roman numeral one
standard abbreviation for south or southern

explanation.surface: Someone takes a stack of books down to a singer from the American South.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Otis Redding, the Georgia soul singer; the question mark admits that OTIS is only one example of a soul singer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Otis Redding was a celebrated American soul performer, so his first name serves as an example of the category.

clue.text: Men must vacate rank Portaloo

indicators.note: to vacate is to leave a place, so the letters for 'men' leave the word for 'rank'

blocks.note: a naval rank above captain
men are OR (other ranks, soldiers who are not officers), and those two letters leave

explanation.surface: The troops are ordered to get out of a smelly portable toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' wants to mean smelly, which fits the toilet, but it is a naval rank, COMMODORE; OR for 'men' (other ranks) comes out. Portaloo is a British brand of portable toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are portable toilets: a chair concealing a chamber pot, standing in for the familiar brand of mobile toilet cabin.

clue.text: Adore getting to the bottom of cold Bud

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom comes after, so 'adore' sits beneath 'cold'

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
to adore is to love

explanation.surface: Someone loves getting to the heart of why their friend Bud is so cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bud' reads as a friend's name; it is the flower bud. The pieces run in reverse clue order because the love goes to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The spice is the dried unopened flower bud of a tropical tree, so the plant term is an accurate description.

clue.text: Book of records omits large and small tools

indicators.note: to omit is to leave something out, so the record book drops the letter for 'large'

blocks.note: a LEDGER is a book of accounts; without L for large it loses its first letter
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A records book that leaves out the large and small tools from its listings.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs 'large and small' as sizes of tools, but 'large' is removed from the book and 'small' is added on as a separate letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn trimmers used to cut a neat border along grass are garden implements, so the plural fits the general word.

clue.text: See you start to rub on behind

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the head of 'rub' is used
one thing placed on another follows it in an across clue, so 'behind' comes first

blocks.note: behind schedule means late
the opening letter of rub

explanation.surface: A cheeky farewell to someone about to rub lotion on a behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' reads as a bottom in the surface but means late, as in behind time.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual goodbyes said when parting from a friend you expect to meet again, informal equivalent phrases.

clue.text: Tired and sad chasing game woman ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of 'woman' counts
what chases comes behind, so 'sad' follows 'game' and the end of 'woman'

blocks.note: rugby union, a crossword stalwart for game
the final letter of woman
feeling down is feeling sad

explanation.surface: A worn-out, miserable man trails after a woman he is pursuing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game woman' looks like a willing partner in the surface, but game is RU and the woman supplies only her last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exhausted and in poor health is described with this adjective, a direct synonym for being worn out.

clue.text: Tory leader mostly tit, judge admitted

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word for 'tit' loses its last letter
something admitted is let in, so 'judge' goes inside the shortened 'tit'

blocks.note: BOOB, slang for a breast or for a fool, cut short
J is the standard abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A rude verdict on a Conservative leader: mostly an idiot, with a judge let in on the joke.
explanation.walkthrough: BoJo is the tabloid nickname of Boris Johnson, Conservative (Tory) prime minister of the UK 2019-22. 'Tit' is a British insult, fitting the surface, and its synonym BOOB loses the final B.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname belongs to Boris Johnson, who led the Conservative Party, so it names one holder of that post.

clue.text: Creating union and groaning is disgusting

indicators.note: something disgusting is foul or corrupted, so the letters of 'groaning is' come out scrambled

blocks.note: the fodder: ten letters, all used

explanation.surface: Someone finds sex and the grunting that goes with it revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' sounds like sexual union in this surface, but the definition is about forming a trade union among workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Recruiting workers into a trade union is called organising, so the verb form describes bringing that union into being.

clue.text: Live sex could result in this hit

blocks.note: to be is to exist, to live
pregnancy after sex ends in childbirth

explanation.surface: A warning that live sex shows could end in a smash hit, or a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle is a cryptic hint rather than a synonym: sex can lead to pregnancy and so to the pains of giving birth. 'Hit' ends the clue as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The older meaning is to beat someone vigorously, as in a thrashing, so it matches the verb for striking.

clue.text: One on bed that might secure a tug?

definitions.text: One on bed that might secure a tug?

blocks.clueFragment: One on bed that might secure a tug?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone lying in bed who could get a sexual favour

blocks.clueFragment: One on bed that might secure a tug?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a heavy weight resting on the sea bed that holds a tugboat in place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tug' is British slang for a sexual act by hand, which the bed invites, but it is a small harbour boat, and the bed is the sea floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships drop this heavy hooked weight to the seabed to hold them still, so it rests there keeping a boat from drifting.

clue.text: Needing rehabilitation, if Carol in a state

indicators.note: rehabilitation rebuilds something broken, so the letters of 'if Carol in a' need to be put back together differently

blocks.note: the fodder: ten letters, all used

explanation.surface: Carol is in such a state that she needs to go to rehab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' reads as a phrase for being distraught, but 'in a' belongs to the fodder and 'state' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the most populous of the fifty American states, on the Pacific coast, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: Virginal blokes will get help inside

indicators.note: 'help' goes inside 'blokes', so the second piece sits within the first

blocks.note: blokes is British slang for men
to help is to aid

explanation.surface: Inexperienced young men are promised some assistance getting started.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virginal' is an adjective, and MAIDEN works as one too, as in a maiden voyage or maiden speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective it means unmarried, untouched or never before tried, the same sense of purity and first experience.

clue.text: Give a cheeky display around republican diplomat and flapper

indicators.note: the cheeky display goes around the republican and the diplomat, enclosing them

blocks.note: to moon is to bare your buttocks as a prank
R, the standard abbreviation for Republican
His Excellency, the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: Someone flashes their bottom at a Republican envoy and a 1920s party girl.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper was a fashionable young woman of the 1920s, which suits the risqué surface; here it is anything that flaps its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: This common waterbird beats its wings to fly, so a cryptic label for a winged creature fits it playfully.

clue.text: Old Italian person sure can't put out

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or displaced, so the letters of 'sure can't' are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the fodder, ignoring the apostrophe: eight letters

explanation.surface: An elderly Italian is quite certain they will not sleep with anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' is slang for agreeing to sex, which sets the surface, but here it tells you to disturb the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Etruria was an ancient civilisation in central Italy before Rome, so its people were Italians of antiquity.

clue.text: City abroad almost unable to see touring queen

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word for 'unable to see' loses its last letter
to tour is to travel around, so the shortened word goes around 'queen'

blocks.note: BLIND without its final D
Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A near-blind traveller takes a queen on a trip to a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' makes clear the city is foreign rather than British, and 'touring' pulls double duty as travel in the surface and enclosure in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The German capital lies outside Britain, so for a British setter it is an overseas metropolis.

clue.text: A poet inhaling bit of opium on a train?

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is its first letter, so only the head of 'opium' is used
to inhale is to take something in, so the poet takes in the letter from 'opium'

blocks.note: kept as it stands
a bard is a poet
the first letter of opium

explanation.surface: A poet smokes a little opium while travelling by rail, like a Romantic on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a train is only one example: you can be aboard any vehicle or ship.
explanation.definitionFit: It means on or in a vehicle such as a ship, plane or carriage, so a passenger in a railway carriage is described.

clue.text: Opportunity to get around court for drug supplier

indicators.note: getting around something means surrounding it, so 'opportunity' encircles 'court'

blocks.note: an opening, as in a door opening for you
CT, the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A dealer looks for a loophole to avoid a court appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug supplier' conjures a dealer on the run from court; the real supplier is the one who writes prescriptions.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical practitioner prescribes medicines to patients, so a physician is quite literally a legitimate source of medication.

clue.text: Chap who measured wind of a brute letting rip

indicators.note: letting rip means going wild and unrestrained, so the letters of 'of a brute' run riot

blocks.note: the fodder: eight letters

explanation.surface: A man assesses how bad the flatulence of a thuggish companion is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' and 'letting rip' suggest breaking wind; Francis Beaufort, a British admiral, devised the scale for measuring wind speed at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The admiral created the scale from calm to hurricane that sailors use to rate the force of gusts, still named after him.

clue.text: Dope stashed in a hollow cavity in bureau

indicators.note: something hollow is empty inside, so 'cavity' keeps only its outside letters
a stash is hidden inside something, so 'dope' goes in between 'a' and the emptied 'cavity'

blocks.note: kept as it stands
gen is British slang for information, like dope
the first and last letters of cavity

explanation.surface: Drugs are found hidden in a secret compartment of a writing desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' is drugs in the surface but inside information here, and 'bureau' is a desk in the surface but an office at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An office or organisation providing a particular service is called both, as in a travel office or employment service.

clue.text: Regret drinking shot served up for villain

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so 'shot' turns over
drinking takes something in, so 'regret' swallows the turned 'shot'

blocks.note: to rue something is to regret it
a shot is a go, an attempt

explanation.surface: A bad guy is sorry about downing a shot that was put in front of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' and 'drinking' paint a bar scene, but a shot is a turn or try, and 'drinking' puts it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A dishonest or unprincipled scoundrel is described with either noun, so these are close synonyms for a wrongdoer.

clue.text: One near cocaine bundles: future queen, perhaps

blocks.note: C is slang shorthand for cocaine
heaps and bundles are both piles or large amounts
Kate, Princess of Wales, expected to become queen consort; 'perhaps' marks her as one example

explanation.surface: Someone standing close to piles of cocaine, like a royal in a tabloid scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Near' means close in the surface but stingy in the definition, a British sense of the word. Kate is the wife of Prince William, heir to the British throne.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old British word for miserly, so a person who is near is a tightwad who hates spending money.

clue.text: A church covering up new outbreaks?

indicators.note: to cover up is to hide something beneath, so 'church' closes over 'new'

blocks.note: kept as it stands
the Church of England
N, the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A church hushes up news of fresh disease outbreaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbreaks' suggests epidemics; the question mark flags the spotty sense, as a teenager's skin breaks out.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin condition produces pimples that erupt on the face, so the plural noun describes its eruptions in a playful way.

clue.text: Anger The Daily Mail, possibly with bit of erotica

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is its first letter, so only the head of 'erotica' is used

blocks.note: rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper; 'possibly' marks the paper as one example
the first letter of erotica

explanation.surface: Stir up the outrage of a British tabloid by adding a little smut.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British tabloid newspaper known for moral outrage; 'Anger' looks like a verb about riling it but is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a strong feeling of fury, with the answer the more violent form of that emotion.

clue.text: Granny in the thrall of Botswanan naturist

indicators.note: something held in the thrall of another is captive inside it, so the answer lies inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters span the join between the two words

explanation.surface: An old lady is under the spell of a nudist from southern Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrall' suggests enchantment, but it means the letters are held captive within 'Botswanan naturist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are affectionate family names for a grandmother, used by children in Britain and Australia.

clue.text: Say no to bit of coke after last month!

indicators.note: one thing after another follows it, so 'bit of coke' comes behind 'last month'

blocks.note: the calendar abbreviation for December, the final month
a line is a single dose of cocaine, snorted

explanation.surface: A New Year resolution: turn down the cocaine after the December parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit of coke' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it is a whole unit of the drug, a line.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse an offer or invitation politely is to turn it down, the same as the phrasal verb for rejecting.
